messages.subject: Re: Mediation SEM - error could not find function ":="
messages.subject_clean: Mediation SEM - error could not find function ":="
messages.body_plain:
> However is this correct/ necessary in a mediation analysis, and should it be combined with the bootstrapping command like I've done above or not?

MLR will correct SEs for the lack of multivariate normality in your data distribution.  The bootstrapping recommendation for mediation has nothing to do with the data distribution; rather, it accounts for the fact that the estimated indirect effect(s) will not be normally distributed around the true parameter(s) across repeated experiments, even if the direct effects are.

Because bootstrapping (a) doesn't assume your data are normally distributed and (b) doesn't assume that statistics are normally distributed, you could use the bootstrap CIs to test hypotheses about all your parameters and use the Bollen-Stine bootstrap to test exact model fit (although there is no bootstrap.  I'm not sure whether MLR or bootstrapping is more efficient because I haven't read a study comparing them, but either of them would free you of the multivariate normality assumption of your data, and bootstrap CIs also free you of the assumption that sample statistics are normally distributed across experiments.

> I'm not really sure what the difference is between the parameter estimates bootstrapping and the bootstrapping command I have used above?

Neither MLR nor bootstrapping affect the point estimates themselves, only the SEs (and by implication, the test statistics).

> In addition, are there any resources to help interpret the output of this mediation analysis? I'm not sure what parts I should be focusing on/writing up??
>

You can interpret any and all of the parameters, but you might only be expected to interpret (and test null hypotheses about) the parameters that address your research questions, depending on your audience (report for an SEM class vs. thesis/dissertation vs. peer-reviewed journal).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: modification indices in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Have you read the reference cited in the manual page for lavTestScore:

   Bentler, P. M., & Chou, C. P. (1993). Some new covariance
   structure model improvement statistics. Sage Focus Editions, 154,
   235-255.

For lavTestScore(scalar.fit, epc=TRUE), you will get three sections:

1) test: this is the global score test (or multivariate Lagrange
Multiplier test), testing the null hypothesis that all the equality
constraints present in 'scalar.fit' hold

2) uni: these are univariate score tests (aka modification indices, or
univariate Lagrange Multiplier tests) testing the null hypothesis that
the individual equality constraints hold

3) epc: these are the expected parameter changes: how will the
parameters in your model change, *if* you release all the equality
constraints (in the 'epc' column); and how would the parameters look
like ('epv' column) if the constraints are released.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Bifactor ESEM in R and Mplus7
messages.subject_clean: Bifactor ESEM in R and Mplus7
messages.body_plain:
It's actually simpler than the example above (which has some typos). The fit indices and loadings are virtually identical to the ones in Mplus. The difference is that the signs of the loadings are opposite: Mplus shows most loadings as positive and few loadings as negative while funRotate shows the reverse pattern.

Here's the script:

#Bifactor ESEM in R
library(semTools)
library(GPArotation)

#Simulate data (with lavaan)

#One general factor and 2 specific factors
set.seed(123456)
sim.model <- 'g=~.4*i1+.4*i2+.4*i3+.4*i4+.4*i5+.4*i6+.4*i7+.4*i8+.4*i9+.4*i10
f1=~.5*i1+.5*i2+.5*i3+.5*i4+.5*i5
f2=~.6*i6+.6*i7+.6*i8+.6*i9+.6*i10
#orthogonal factors
g~~0*f1+0*f2
f1~~0*f2'
d <- simulateData(model=sim.model, model.type = "cfa", sample.nobs = 200)

#extract 3 unrotated factors: g + 2 specific factors
unrotated <- efaUnrotate(d, nf = 3)
summary(unrotated)

#test model fit as you would in lavaan

fitMeasures(unrotated, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "srmr", "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "bic"))

#Create a target matrix
target <- matrix(0, 10, 3)
target[1:10, 1] <- NA #general factor
target[1:5, 2] <- NA #group factor
target[6:10, 3] <- NA #group factor
target

#Target rotation (orthogonal)
rotated <- funRotate(unrotated, fun="targetT", Target=target)

#Output
round(rotated@loading, 3)

messages.body_plain:
The different sign does not really matter. It is the nature of factor indeterimancy. You may reverse the sign by hand.

CAUTION: SE resulting from factor rotation in semToools is currently invalid. It does not account for the instability of the results from factor rotation. It is just based on delta method. Therefore, please do not trust the standard error or test statistic of the rotated statistics.

messages.subject: Re: Can I calculate Log-Likelihood values in model with WLSMV estimator?
messages.subject_clean: Can I calculate Log-Likelihood values in model with WLSMV estimator?
messages.body_plain:
WLSMV and friends (DWLS, WLS, GLS, ULS, with or without MV) are
estimation methods based on least squares. There is simply no likelihood
involved. So there can not be a (log)likelihood, or any other measure
that depends on it: AIC and BIC.

Yves.

On 06/01/2016 04:29 PM, Nicolas Richard wrote:
> Same problem, looking to get BIC or AIC but can't, Any alternative with

messages.subject: basic question - residual covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

I want to compute the residual covariance matrix manually, but I think I am doing something wrong.
Suppose that this is my model:

my.model <- '
# Measurement model
Y1 =~ 1 * y1
Y2 =~ 1 * y2
Y3 =~ 1 * y3

# measurement error
y1 ~~ 0.10 * y1
y2 ~~ 0.02 * y2
y3 ~~ 0.05 * y3

# structural model
Y1 ~ x1 + x2
Y2 ~ x3 + x4
Y3 ~ Y1 + Y2

# error variance
Y1 ~~ Y2
'
my.fit <- sem(my.model, fixed.x = TRUE, data = data)

x1 to x4 are deterministic variables, so they have not variance and phi is zero. The data is "y1", "y2", "y3", "x1", "x2", "x3", "x4". All variables were standardized.
Now I want to see the residual covariance matrix of the endogenous variables (Y1, Y2, Y3), so:

B <- inspect(my.fit, "est")$beta[1:3,1:3] # beta coefficients
I <- diag(nrow = 3, ncol = 3) # lambda_y coefficients
A <- inspect(my.fit, "est")$beta[1:3,4:7] # gamma coefficients
V <- inspect(my.fit.lv.ML <http://my.fit.lv.ML>, "est")$psi[1:3,1:3] # Psi coefficients
Th <- inspect(my.fit.lv.ML <http://my.fit.lv.ML>, "est")$theta[1:3,1:3] #theta coefficients
IB <- solve(I - B)

SigmaHat <- (IB %*% V %*% t(IB)) + Th
S <- cov(data[,1:3])
Residuals <- S - SigmaHat

Why Residuals is not equal to residuals(my.fit, "raw")$cov[1:3,1:3]?

Thanks in advance,

Marcos

Marcos--
     Which residual covariance matrix do you want? "psi" IS the residual covariance matrix for the "factors" (Y1, Y2, Y3) while "theta" IS the residual covariance matrix for the observed variables y1, y2, y3. You have specified the residual variances for y1, y2, y3 by assignment. At the same time, you specified that Y1, Y2, Y3 are not strictly equivalent to y1, y2, y3.

messages.subject_clean: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.body_plain:
> Read about longitudinal CFA and multitrait-multimethod models for ideas about handling dependent measures like this.  Essentially, you can put the data in wide format (the same indicator will be in multiple columns, one for each within-subjects condition).  Then define the each factor separately for each condition (e.g., Factor1_type1, Factor2_type1, Factor1_type2, Factor2_type2) and also define a method factor for each indicator to account for item-specific variance that is constant across conditions.

As a quick follow-up to this, should I also specify a second level factor for each original factor, i.e.

Factor1 =~ Factor1_type1 + Factor1_type2 + Factor1_type3 + Factor1_type4
... etc.

as a representation of the factor across conditions?

Thank you again.

On Thursday, May 26, 2016 at 3:21:13 AM UTC-6, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > ...(1.000 power for nearly all comparisons). Do you have any idea what could be going wrong, or are the results actually accurate (N=200 sufficient for power analysis), or am I misinterpreting the output?
>
> Hard to know if that should be surprising.  By comparisons, I assume you are talking about a likelihood ratio test (chi-squared difference between nested models).  If you put your population values into matrices (like you do for the popParam argument in simsem::bind), you can calculate the population mean vector and covariance matrix using matrix algebra.  Then fit any model to the population moments using the sample.cov and sample.means arguments (setting sample.nobs to any arbitrary value).  Then you can extract the model-implied moments from the model fit, and use simsem::popDiscrepancy() to calculate population-level discrepancy measures (RMSEA, SRMR, and minimum ML fit function) of the model.
>
> > M1 <- intercepts + Lambda %*% Alpha
> > S1 <- Lambda %*% Psi %*% t(Lambda) + Theta
> > fit0 <- lavaan(model, sample.cov = S1, sample.means = M1, sample.nobs = 200)
> > M0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "mean.ov")
> > S0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "cov.ov")
> > popDiscrepancy(paramM = M1, paramCM = S1, misspecM = M0, misspecCM = S0)
>
> That takes sampling error out of the equation and let's you see a descriptive measure of model misfit.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

In my current analysis, I'm running through a problem. In one of my MGCFA models, using the original cognitive subtest variables, I got the error message "lavaan WARNING: model has NOT converged!" whereas when I correct for age and gender effects, the model has converged. I have no idea what happened and how to interpret this outcome.

Here's what the syntax looks like :

setwd("c:\\Users\\R")
entiredata<-read.csv("Woodcock-Johnson Murray_2007.csv")

require(lavaan)
require(psy)

entiredata3<- subset(entiredata, racesample<3 & wj==3 & sample==1)
require(dplyr)
d3<- select(entiredata3, testage, sex, racesample, sample, wj, c02spatrels, c04visaudit, c05blend, c06verbcomp, c07vismatch, c09analsyn, c10numrev, c11concform, c13picrecog, c14memwords, c15geninfo, c16retrieve, c17audatten, c18decisions)
d3 = d3[complete.cases(d3),]

m1<- lm(c02spatrels~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$spatrels<-residuals(m1)
m2<- lm(c04visaudit~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$visaudit<-residuals(m2)
m3<- lm(c05blend~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$blend<-residuals(m3)
m4<- lm(c06verbcomp~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$verbcomp<-residuals(m4)
m5<- lm(c07vismatch~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$vismatch<-residuals(m5)
m6<- lm(c09analsyn~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$analsyn<-residuals(m6)
m7<- lm(c10numrev~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$numrev<-residuals(m7)
m8<- lm(c11concform~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$concform<-residuals(m8)
m9<- lm(c13picrecog~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$picrecog<-residuals(m9)
m10<- lm(c14memwords~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$memwords<-residuals(m10)
m11<- lm(c15geninfo~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$geninfo<-residuals(m11)
m12<- lm(c16retrieve~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$retrieve<-residuals(m12)
m13<- lm(c17audatten~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$audatten<-residuals(m13)
m14<- lm(c18decisions~ testage+sex, data=d3, weights=d3$weight)
d3$decisions<-residuals(m14)

dgroup3<-select(d3, racesample, sample, wj, spatrels, visaudit, blend, verbcomp, vismatch, analsyn, numrev, concform, picrecog, memwords, geninfo, retrieve, audatten, decisions)

combined.commonfactor14.model <-'
Gc =~ c06verbcomp + c15geninfo
Gf =~ c02spatrels + c04visaudit + c09analsyn + c11concform + c13picrecog
Gsm =~ c05blend + c10numrev + c14memwords
Gs=~ c07vismatch + c16retrieve + c17audatten + c18decisions
Gs ~ 0*1
'

commonfactor14.fit<-cfa(combined.commonfactor14.model, data=d3, group="racesample", meanstructure=TRUE, group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"), group.partial=c("Gc~~Gc", "Gf~~Gf", "Gsm~~Gsm", "Gc~~Gf", "Gc~~Gsm", "Gf~~Gsm"))
fitMeasures(commonfactor14.fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr", "aic", "bic"))

combined.commonfactor14.model <-'
Gc =~ verbcomp + geninfo
Gf =~ spatrels + visaudit + analsyn + concform + picrecog
Gsm =~ blend + numrev + memwords
Gs =~ vismatch + retrieve + audatten + decisions
Gs ~ 0*1
'

commonfactor14.fit<-cfa(combined.commonfactor14.model, data=dgroup3, group="racesample", meanstructure=TRUE, group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"), group.partial=c("Gc~~Gc", "Gf~~Gf", "Gsm~~Gsm", "Gc~~Gf", "Gc~~Gsm", "Gf~~Gsm"))
fitMeasures(commonfactor14.fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr", "aic", "bic"))

It's also curious that the model fit among other models are very close when using uncorrected variables compared to when using corrected variables.

Any help is appreciated.

Thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
>         Why Residuals is not equal to residuals(my.fit, "raw")$cov[1:3,1:3]?

Two things: you need the full matrices, including the x's (not just the
first three rows/cols), and S is divided by N (not N-1):

attach(inspect(my.fit, "est"))
IB.inv <- solve(diag( nrow(beta) ) - beta)
Sigma.hat <- lambda %*% IB.inv %*% psi %*% t(IB.inv) %*% t(lambda) + theta
# should be the same as fitted(my.fit)$cov

# sample cov (divided by N, instead of N-1)
S <- cov(Data[,lavNames(my.fit)]) * (nobs(my.fit) - 1) / nobs(my.fit)

# residuals
Sigma.hat - S
# resid(my.fit)$cov

Yves.

I have no idea what is going on, but a couple oddities I noticed:
You don't seem to select() a "weight" variable when you create d3, but you use it in your lm() calls.  Is that a sampling weight that needs to be accounted for in your CFA, too?  If so, look into the lavaan.survey package.
You are fitting a highly restrictive model.  Have you fit a configural model to see if it converges when you allow estimates to differ across groups?  Typically, those measurement-invariance constraints are sequentially tested one set at a time, to make sure those assumptions hold.  Look into the measurementInvariance() function in the semTools package.
Instead of running 14 regressions, you could (and maybe should) regress the indicators on age and sex in your CFA.  The way you are doing it assumes that the effects of age and sex are constant across the groups in your CFA, which might not be the case.  Including those controls in your CFA would allow you to test the assumption that they are equivalent by including "regressions" in your group.equal argument and testing whether model fit is worse.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Correlation between Latent Variables
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to fit a full structural equation model consisting of a measurement model and a latent variable model. The measurement model is made of three latent factor which are measured by 12 indicators. In the latent variable model, I regress two of the factors on the third factor. My data is multivariate Normal. Since I am new to Lavaan, I have tried two approaches to this end.

In the first attempt I manually define the correlations between the factors AND set orthogonal=TRUE. The syntax I am using follows:

model.sem<-'f3=~X1+X2+X3+X4
f1=~X5+X6+X7+X8
f2=~X9+X10+X11+X12
f3 ~~ f1
f3 ~~ f2
f1 ~~ f2
f1 ~~ 1*f1
f2 ~~ 1*f2
f3 ~~ 1*f3
f1=~X4
f3 ~ f1 + f2
'
model.sem.fit<-sem(model.sem,data=data,orthogonal=TRUE, estimator="ML",std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,std.ov = TRUE)

After running the syntax, Lavaan warns that the model is not identified.

However, when I do not manually set the correlations and use orthogonal=FALSE the model then runs perfectly fine. The syntax follows:

model.sem<-'f3=~X1+X2+X3+X4
f1=~X5+X6+X7+X8
f2=~X9+X10+X11+X12
f1=~X4
f3 ~ f1 + f2
'

model.sem.fit<-sem(model.sem,data=data,estimator="ML",std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,std.ov = TRUE)

I am still relatively new to SEM so please excuse me if I am missing the obvious.

Any help would be appreciated.

Regards,

Linniker Grech

messages.subject: Autoregressive model with binary variable
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Currently I'm trying to fit an autoregressive model that contains 4 constructs measured over time (I have 3 measurement points). Some of the variables are not normally distributed, so I prefer to use robust estimation.
One of the constructs (that also has repeated measurements) is binary, and I declared this one as ordered for measurements 2 and 3 (not for the first measurement, because it's an exogenous variable there). Because of these ordered variables I used DWLS estimation instead of maximum likelihood, as suggested by lavaan.

I want to include the covariances between the variables at each measurement, including the covariances between the exogenous variables at measurement 1. For this I used fixed.x = FALSE. This works well as long as I don't declare any variables as ordered, but it's incompatible with DWLS estimation. It does work with ULSM and ULSMV, but I'm not sure which one to use. I understand that ULSM results in a mean adjusted test statistic, and that ULSMV results in a test statistic that is mean and variance adjusted. In line with that, the choice between ULSM and ULSMV does not affect model parameters, but it does affect the robust model chi square and other robust fit indices (CFI, RMSEA), with ULSM leading to better CFI values, and ULSMV yielding better chi squared and RMSEA values.

If anyone has any thoughts on whether to use ULSM or ULSMV in this situation, or can suggest criteria to base my choice on, that would be greatly appreciated!
Thanks in advance,

Best wishes,

Eline Ensing

P.S. This is the model syntax that I used (w6 is measurement 1, w7 is measurement 2, and w8 is measurement 3; and the FR42305 are binary, with F measured at measurement 1, G at 2, and H at 3):

AUTO.Model1 <- '
  #AUTOREGRESSIONS
  #Smoker identity
    SmokSelf_w8 ~ SmokSelf_w7
    SmokSelf_w7 ~ SmokSelf_w6
  #Quitter identity
    QuitSelf_w8 ~ QuitSelf_w7
    QuitSelf_w7 ~ QuitSelf_w6
  #Smoker group-identity
    SmokGroup_w8 ~ SmokGroup_w7
    SmokGroup_w7 ~ SmokGroup_w6
  #Behavior
    hFR42305 ~ gFR42305
    gFR42305 ~ fFR42305
  #COVARIANCES
      SmokSelf_w7 ~~ QuitSelf_w7
      SmokSelf_w7 ~~ SmokGroup_w7
      SmokSelf_w7 ~~ gFR42305
      QuitSelf_w7 ~~ SmokGroup_w7
      QuitSelf_w7 ~~ gFR42305
      SmokGroup_w7 ~~ gFR42305
'

AUTO.Model1a.fit <- sem(AUTO.Model1, data=DataITC2, meanstructure=T, estimator="ULSMV",fixed.x=FALSE, ordered=c('gFR42305','hFR42305'))
AUTO.Model1b.fit <- sem(AUTO.Model1, data=DataITC2, meanstructure=T, estimator="ULSM",fixed.x=FALSE, ordered=c('gFR42305','hFR42305'))

Hi,

I am new to SEM and Lavaan and I am trying to understand that the approach I am using is justifiable. I would be really grateful for any feedback on the below.

Having previously performed confirmatory factor analysis, I am now conducting a mediation analysis using the latent variables. My aim is to use bootstrapping and effect sizes rather than a causal steps/sobel test approach:

SCTModel2 <- 'PF1=~pers2+pers4+pers3+pers8+pers7

BehF1=~BF1+BF2+BF3+BF4+BF6+BF7

EnvF1=~Env1+Env3+Env4+Env5

 # direct effect

             BehF1 ~ c*PF1

           # mediator

            EnvF1 ~ a*PF1

           # total effect

         '

SCTfit<-sem(SCTModel2, data = SMBI_Alldata, estimator="MLR",bootstrap = 5000)

messages.subject: Re: Correlation between Latent Variables
messages.body_plain:
> isn't that what orthogonal=FALSE does? It allows the latent variables to be correlated.

Yes, that sets the default behavior, but the model syntax overrides any defaults you turn on/off (e.g., you can set std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE but still free some latent variances using f1 ~~ NA*f1, although that might cause identification issues).

So in your first example, you set orthogonal = TRUE (which omitted latent covariances from the parameter table by default), but the covariances you specified in the model syntax were still then added to the parameter table anyway.  If you don't want to estimate them, leave them out of the syntax (or set them to 0 in the syntax: f1 ~~ 0*f2).

In your second example, you didn't specify any latent covariances in your model syntax, but you left orthogonal set to its default setting (FALSE), so the covariances among your exogenous latent variables were added to the parameter table by default.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: SEM Mediation - Indirect Effect Size
messages.body_plain:
> Is it normal/ recommended to report to model fit statistics (e.g. CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) for a mediation analysis in a PhD thesis?

Yes, for any non-saturated SEM you would be expected to address whether the model appears consistent with how the data were generated from a population process.

> Also what has the 'bootstrap = 5000' command actually done here as I can't see any reference to bootstrapping in my output?

If you set test = "bollen.stine", you would see a bootstrap p value for the chi-squared test of perfect model fit.  Although the labels don't change, the SEs are the SDs of the bootstrap distribution, not calculated from the covariance matrix of the model parameters.  But in your sem() call, you should also explicitly set se = "boot" if that is what you want.

> If I've understood this correctly, the regression shows  b is not significant and so you would conclude no mediation rather than carry on at this stage (do you need a, b and c to be significant)? In addition the indirect effect is not significant so you would conclude no mediation? Or have I misinterpreted this?
>

I thought you said you weren't following those steps (and that you were interested in effect sizes, not tests)?  Whether a particular direct effect is significant at an arbitrary alpha level is a function of sample size and effect size, so it is not necessarily the case that "b" is truly zero in the population, just that the data you have don't allow you to distinguish the estimated effect from zero.  For testing the null hypothesis that the indirect effect is zero in the population, I would only check test the relevant parameter: the indirect effect (which is also not significant in your case).  But this isn't software specific, so you might find different advice if you post your question on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> (a more general forum with a wider audience of SEM experts).

> Supposing my data did suggest mediation, my understanding is that R uses the Sobel (delta) approach to calculating the indirect effect

"R" does lots of things in lots of different packages.  The lavaan package will give you delta-method SEs (for a Sobel test) by default, if you don't request bootstrap SEs.

>
> This shows that the 95% confidence interval for the indirect effect is (-.003, .045) - is that all you would report from this output?

If that is the only hypothesis you are interested in testing, then the CI will give you a way to test it (whether zero is in the CI).

> How would I generate the effect size of an indirect effect using R - I understand that kappa squared is a good but I'm unsure if R allows me to do this?

R doesn't prevent you from doing anything.  If you know the formula and can extract the relevant information from your results, you can calculate it.  But the standardized slopes (std.all) you requested in your summary output are also effect sizes: they tell you how many SDs the outcome changes when the predictor goes up by 1 SD.

> Also - I know that bollen-stine bootstrap could test the model fit - what exactly are the advantages of this? Should this be added to my initial command when fitting the model to give me a different model fit output and what is the command in lavaan for this?

You can set test = "bollen.stine".  The advantage is that it bases the p value on a null hypothesis that is actually true because the data are rescaled to be perfectly consistent with estimated model parameters before bootstrapping and fitting the model to each bootstrapped sample.  If you bootstrapped the chi-squared test statistic without that transformation, then the mean and variance of that bootstrap distribution would follow the observed data-model fit, so the resulting bootstrap distribution would not be a valid distribution for testing the null hypothesis of perfect model fit.

Note that if you are using the Bollen-Stine bootstrap and the bootstrap CIs for all tests, then you don't need to set estimator = "MLR" because bootstrapping already does not rely on the assumption of normality.  But if you are only interested in bootstrap CIs for the indirect effects, then the robust SEs and robust chi-squared under MLR provide valid tests.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: sempath & fixed factor loading
messages.body_plain:
> Regarding the residual, the diagram shown had a two-headed arrow pointing to each indicator. Is that error or disturbance term associated with that indicator? I have seen paper drawing a separate oval for that. Are they the same thing? If so, which is preferred?

Yes, that is shorthand for saving space, but it represents the same thing as actually drawing the residual/disturbance term as an explicit latent variable with a factor loading fixed to 1.  Either way, the tracing rules for the double-headed arrow lead to the same model-implied covariance matrix.

> 2. I am using Lavaan and the factor loading of the first indicator of a latent variable is fixed to 1. But I also see other paper showing the SE, Z-value and p-value for that first indicator. I might be conceptually unclear. Where can I find this information or it can be ignored?

It sounds like in the paper you refer to, they might identify the factor variance by fixing it to 1 instead of freely estimating the factor variance and fixing an arbitrary factor loading to 1.  Both are acceptable and lead to the same model-implied covariance matrix and model fit, but the SEs (and by implication, z tests) are sensitive to which factor loading you fix to 1 (see reference <http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.6.3.258>).  So unless you have a substantive reason for choosing a particular indicator to use as the reference for setting the scale of the latent variable, then I would typically recommend fixing the factor variance to 1.  But that is not a software-specific question, so you might want to seek advice on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> (a larger and more general SEM forum).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Non convergence in MGCFA with original vars and convergence with vars corrected for covariates
messages.body_plain:
> Is the syntax correct?

Yes

> I have compared the output with the model syntax that does not include testage and sex variables as covariates, and the former model fits the data better. So, I suppose I have to conclude that gender and age effects don't matter at all in group differences.

Well, that is the wrong conclusion because the models are not fit to the same data if they don't include the same variables.  First, you wanted to control for the effects of age and sex, so you don't need to compare model fit between models with and without them.  If you want to know whether age and sex have significant effects, look at the tests and effect sizes of those regression coefficients.  Second, in addition to the model you ran, you should also fit the model (i.e., using the same syntax) without including "regressions" in the "group.equal" vector.  Then, use anova() to compare the fit of those nested models to test your assumption that those regression coefficients are equal across groups.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics

messages.subject: Re: Optimization in FIML
messages.body_plain:
> I am very interested in understanding how this optimization is performed. Do you use gradient based methods, and if so which one(s)?

With complete data, the sum of each individual row's log-likelihoods leads to the same ML fit function as the complete-data shortcut using summary data:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-IHRzL6lk2to/V1U7bRJjBsI/AAAAAAAAACc/JZ31HAUFNyE9MrTADJoXZbuBOejBh_BaQCLcB/s1600/MLwithMeans.png>

So it is really the same quantity that is being minimized, except that you can't use the shortcut formula when there are missing data.  If you look at the "control" argument on lavaan's help page (?lavaan), you can see what lavaan's default optimizers are using unconstrained and constrained estimation, and there are links to the help pages for those.  Although they do use gradient methods, I don't think the help pages provide much info (I don't see a References section there), but perhaps Prof. Rosseel could offer more details.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Monday, June 6, 2016 at 4:47:43 PM UTC+8, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>
> > Regarding the residual, the diagram shown had a two-headed arrow pointing to each indicator. Is that error or disturbance term associated with that indicator? I have seen paper drawing a separate oval for that. Are they the same thing? If so, which is preferred?
>
> Yes, that is shorthand for saving space, but it represents the same thing as actually drawing the residual/disturbance term as an explicit latent variable with a factor loading fixed to 1.  Either way, the tracing rules for the double-headed arrow lead to the same model-implied covariance matrix.
>
> > 2. I am using Lavaan and the factor loading of the first indicator of a latent variable is fixed to 1. But I also see other paper showing the SE, Z-value and p-value for that first indicator. I might be conceptually unclear. Where can I find this information or it can be ignored?
>
> It sounds like in the paper you refer to, they might identify the factor variance by fixing it to 1 instead of freely estimating the factor variance and fixing an arbitrary factor loading to 1.  Both are acceptable and lead to the same model-implied covariance matrix and model fit, but the SEs (and by implication, z tests) are sensitive to which factor loading you fix to 1 (see reference <http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.6.3.258>).  So unless you have a substantive reason for choosing a particular indicator to use as the reference for setting the scale of the latent variable, then I would typically recommend fixing the factor variance to 1.  But that is not a software-specific question, so you might want to seek advice on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> (a larger and more general SEM forum).

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ed and Yves,

I have one more question about this topic. In the example that I provided Xs are deterministic variables ( ξ ~ N( ζ,0) ), so I set fixed.x = TRUE in the sem() function. However, when you estimate Sigma.hat you consider Xs as random variables, as phi (which are the values for Xs in psi lavaan matrix) is not zero. Please, could you explain why is that?

I leave a small example that anyone can reproduce

library(lavaan)
rm(list=ls())
x <- rnorm(1000,1,1)
y <- 0.5*x + rnorm(1000,0.1,1)
z <- 1.2*x + rnorm(1000,0.1,1)
d <- data.frame(x=x,y=y,z=z)

model <- '
y ~ x
z ~ x
y ~~ 0 * z
'
my.fit <- sem(model, data = d, meanstructure = F, fixed.x = T)
summary(my.fit)

attach(inspect(my.fit, "est"))
beta
lambda
psi # here, if x is deterministic (fixed.x=T), should x ~~ x equal zero?
theta

IB.inv <- solve(diag( nrow(beta) ) - beta)

IB.inv

Sigma.hat <- lambda %*% IB.inv %*% psi %*% t(IB.inv) %*% t(lambda) + theta

Sigma.hat

I really appreciate hour help.
Kind regards,
Marcos

> >         Why Residuals is not equal to residuals(my.fit, "raw")$cov[1:3,1:3]?

> Two things: you need the full matrices, including the x's (not just the
> first three rows/cols), and S is divided by N (not N-1):
>
> attach(inspect(my.fit, "est"))
> IB.inv <- solve(diag( nrow(beta) ) - beta)
> Sigma.hat <- lambda %*% IB.inv %*% psi %*% t(IB.inv) %*% t(lambda) + theta
> # should be the same as fitted(my.fit)$cov
>
> # sample cov (divided by N, instead of N-1)
> S <- cov(Data[,lavNames(my.fit)]) * (nobs(my.fit) - 1) / nobs(my.fit)
>
> # residuals
> Sigma.hat - S
> # resid(my.fit)$cov
>
> Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Causal indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> On 07 Jun 2016, at 20:46 , David Roaché <daro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you, Mikko! I'm trying to figure out why my formative indicator isn't identified. So, I turned off the covariances between the exogenous variables (or at least I think so). I'm receiving the following errors:
>
> Warning messages:
> 1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, group.label = group.label,  :
>   lavaan WARNING: all observed variables are exogenous; model may not be identified
> 2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
>   lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
>   lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.
>
> Here is my model syntax:
>
> freq1 <- '
> TMC_P <~ 1*FREQ2_P+FREQ3_P+FREQ4_P+FREQ5_P+FREQ6_P+FREQ7_P
> '
>
> fit <- cfa(freq1, data = dat, fixed.x=FALSE)

Your model is basically a regression model where the dependent variable is not observed.

>
> I've read elsewhere in this group that it may not be advisable to include a formative indicator without another indicator (i.e. reflexive or formative). Is it possible that this is also contributing to the identification issue?

Yes. To identify a model, you need to observe either multiple effects to infer a common cause (a factor) or observe a cause and an effect. Observing multiple causes but no effect will not allow you to say anything. To identify a causal indicator model, you need at least one effect indicator.

A common practice is to include two indicators, but this actually makes the latent variable a common factor (“reflective”) and the causal indicator part of the model becomes redundant and can be left out. I have a forthcoming paper about this issue.

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303725610_Omission_of_causal_indicators_Consequences_and_implications_for_measurement

More generally, using formative models is a really bad idea. Typically you aggregate indicators representing multiple dimensions into one score. Except in very unusual scenarios, this scores is uninterpretable. Consider an example of a formative variable “personss size”, defined as a sum of height (kg) and weight (cm). My “person’s size” is about 250, but that does not really tell anything useful: you cannot buy me pants or give dietary recommendations because a tall and thin person would have the same score as a short and fat person.

Edwards summarizes this and many other arguments in this paper:

Edwards, J. R. (2011). The Fallacy of Formative Measurement. Organizational Research Methods, 14(2), 370–388. http://doi.org/10.1177/1094428110378369

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: SEM Mediation - Indirect Effect Size
messages.body_plain:
This is really really helpful and makes things a lot clearer to me - thank you!

On 6 June 2016 at 09:39, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Is it normal/ recommended to report to model fit statistics (e.g. CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) for a mediation analysis in a PhD thesis?
>
> Yes, for any non-saturated SEM you would be expected to address whether the model appears consistent with how the data were generated from a population process.
>
> > Also what has the 'bootstrap = 5000' command actually done here as I can't see any reference to bootstrapping in my output?
>
> If you set test = "bollen.stine", you would see a bootstrap p value for the chi-squared test of perfect model fit.  Although the labels don't change, the SEs are the SDs of the bootstrap distribution, not calculated from the covariance matrix of the model parameters.  But in your sem() call, you should also explicitly set se = "boot" if that is what you want.
>
> > If I've understood this correctly, the regression shows  b is not significant and so you would conclude no mediation rather than carry on at this stage (do you need a, b and c to be significant)? In addition the indirect effect is not significant so you would conclude no mediation? Or have I misinterpreted this?
> >
>
> I thought you said you weren't following those steps (and that you were interested in effect sizes, not tests)?  Whether a particular direct effect is significant at an arbitrary alpha level is a function of sample size and effect size, so it is not necessarily the case that "b" is truly zero in the population, just that the data you have don't allow you to distinguish the estimated effect from zero.  For testing the null hypothesis that the indirect effect is zero in the population, I would only check test the relevant parameter: the indirect effect (which is also not significant in your case).  But this isn't software specific, so you might find different advice if you post your question on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> (a more general forum with a wider audience of SEM experts).
>
> > Supposing my data did suggest mediation, my understanding is that R uses the Sobel (delta) approach to calculating the indirect effect
>
> "R" does lots of things in lots of different packages.  The lavaan package will give you delta-method SEs (for a Sobel test) by default, if you don't request bootstrap SEs.
>
> >
> > This shows that the 95% confidence interval for the indirect effect is (-.003, .045) - is that all you would report from this output?
>
> If that is the only hypothesis you are interested in testing, then the CI will give you a way to test it (whether zero is in the CI).
>
> > How would I generate the effect size of an indirect effect using R - I understand that kappa squared is a good but I'm unsure if R allows me to do this?
>
> R doesn't prevent you from doing anything.  If you know the formula and can extract the relevant information from your results, you can calculate it.  But the standardized slopes (std.all) you requested in your summary output are also effect sizes: they tell you how many SDs the outcome changes when the predictor goes up by 1 SD.
>
> > Also - I know that bollen-stine bootstrap could test the model fit - what exactly are the advantages of this? Should this be added to my initial command when fitting the model to give me a different model fit output and what is the command in lavaan for this?
>
> You can set test = "bollen.stine".  The advantage is that it bases the p value on a null hypothesis that is actually true because the data are rescaled to be perfectly consistent with estimated model parameters before bootstrapping and fitting the model to each bootstrapped sample.  If you bootstrapped the chi-squared test statistic without that transformation, then the mean and variance of that bootstrap distribution would follow the observed data-model fit, so the resulting bootstrap distribution would not be a valid distribution for testing the null hypothesis of perfect model fit.
>
> Note that if you are using the Bollen-Stine bootstrap and the bootstrap CIs for all tests, then you don't need to set estimator = "MLR" because bootstrapping already does not rely on the assumption of normality.  But if you are only interested in bootstrap CIs for the indirect effects, then the robust SEs and robust chi-squared under MLR provide valid tests.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Re: Causal indicators
messages.body_plain:
H
i

>
> On 07 Jun 2016, at 22:14 , David Roaché <daro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for sending along these great resources. My dilemma is that the construct I am trying to model is theoretically comprised of all of the items (they refer to communication frequency across different communication media; i.e., text message, phone calls, etc.). Removing one item seems at odds with what the communication literature tells me; however, if I am reading your paper correctly, omitting an item or items does not actually influence the estimates when examining the latent variable's relationship with other latent variables in the structural. So, it's actually better to simply run my model as a reflective indicator, yes?

No. In this case you can think that the construct is simply the sum of frequencies: if I call you 2 times in a week and send 3 emails, our communications frequency is 5 contacts per week. Just take a sum of the variables and use the sum instead of the original variables in your SEM model.

In your case creating a sum makes sense. Summing indicators is a good analysis strategy, which only becomes problematic if you specify the sum inside SEM software, estimate the weights from the data, and add an error term to make the sum a latent variable (i.e. when you use causal indicators.)

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: Causal indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you use an agreement scale, you would ideally take unreliability (random measurement error) into account in your model. But in your case this does not seem to be possible, so I would just use a sum or mean of the items. It is a really robust way to construct indices. See e.g.

Bobko, P., Roth, P. L., & Buster, M. A. (2007). The usefulness of unit weights in creating composite scores: A literature review, application to content validity, and meta-analysis. Organizational Research Methods, 10(4), 689–709. http://doi.org/10.1177/1094428106294734

and the reference therein.

If you want further opinions on this, you can also try posting on the SEMNET email list.

Mikko

messages.subject: Re: SEM Mediation - Indirect Effect Size
messages.body_plain:
Just one quick think to clarify - would you use test = ''bollen.stine'' and se = boot or does the bolen stine test replace the need for se = boot?

Thanks

Emma.

On 7 June 2016 at 19:51, Emma Mills <emmami...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> This is really really helpful and makes things a lot clearer to me - thank you!
>
> On 6 June 2016 at 09:39, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Is it normal/ recommended to report to model fit statistics (e.g. CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) for a mediation analysis in a PhD thesis?
> >
> > Yes, for any non-saturated SEM you would be expected to address whether the model appears consistent with how the data were generated from a population process.
> >
> > > Also what has the 'bootstrap = 5000' command actually done here as I can't see any reference to bootstrapping in my output?
> >
> > If you set test = "bollen.stine", you would see a bootstrap p value for the chi-squared test of perfect model fit.  Although the labels don't change, the SEs are the SDs of the bootstrap distribution, not calculated from the covariance matrix of the model parameters.  But in your sem() call, you should also explicitly set se = "boot" if that is what you want.
> >
> > > If I've understood this correctly, the regression shows  b is not significant and so you would conclude no mediation rather than carry on at this stage (do you need a, b and c to be significant)? In addition the indirect effect is not significant so you would conclude no mediation? Or have I misinterpreted this?
> > >
> >
> > I thought you said you weren't following those steps (and that you were interested in effect sizes, not tests)?  Whether a particular direct effect is significant at an arbitrary alpha level is a function of sample size and effect size, so it is not necessarily the case that "b" is truly zero in the population, just that the data you have don't allow you to distinguish the estimated effect from zero.  For testing the null hypothesis that the indirect effect is zero in the population, I would only check test the relevant parameter: the indirect effect (which is also not significant in your case).  But this isn't software specific, so you might find different advice if you post your question on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> (a more general forum with a wider audience of SEM experts).
> >
> > > Supposing my data did suggest mediation, my understanding is that R uses the Sobel (delta) approach to calculating the indirect effect
> >
> > "R" does lots of things in lots of different packages.  The lavaan package will give you delta-method SEs (for a Sobel test) by default, if you don't request bootstrap SEs.
> >
> > >
> > > This shows that the 95% confidence interval for the indirect effect is (-.003, .045) - is that all you would report from this output?
> >
> > If that is the only hypothesis you are interested in testing, then the CI will give you a way to test it (whether zero is in the CI).
> >
> > > How would I generate the effect size of an indirect effect using R - I understand that kappa squared is a good but I'm unsure if R allows me to do this?
> >
> > R doesn't prevent you from doing anything.  If you know the formula and can extract the relevant information from your results, you can calculate it.  But the standardized slopes (std.all) you requested in your summary output are also effect sizes: they tell you how many SDs the outcome changes when the predictor goes up by 1 SD.
> >
> > > Also - I know that bollen-stine bootstrap could test the model fit - what exactly are the advantages of this? Should this be added to my initial command when fitting the model to give me a different model fit output and what is the command in lavaan for this?
> >
> > You can set test = "bollen.stine".  The advantage is that it bases the p value on a null hypothesis that is actually true because the data are rescaled to be perfectly consistent with estimated model parameters before bootstrapping and fitting the model to each bootstrapped sample.  If you bootstrapped the chi-squared test statistic without that transformation, then the mean and variance of that bootstrap distribution would follow the observed data-model fit, so the resulting bootstrap distribution would not be a valid distribution for testing the null hypothesis of perfect model fit.
> >
> > Note that if you are using the Bollen-Stine bootstrap and the bootstrap CIs for all tests, then you don't need to set estimator = "MLR" because bootstrapping already does not rely on the assumption of normality.  But if you are only interested in bootstrap CIs for the indirect effects, then the robust SEs and robust chi-squared under MLR provide valid tests.

On 06/07/2016 04:25 PM, Marcos Angelini wrote:
> Dear Ed and Yves,
>
> I have one more question about this topic. In the example that I
> provided Xs are deterministic variables ( ξ ~ N( ζ,0) ), so I set
> fixed.x = TRUE in the sem() function. However, when you estimate
> Sigma.hat you consider Xs as random variables

No, we do not.

as phi (which are the
> values for Xs in psi lavaan matrix) is not zero.

The values in psi simply reflect the observed (sample)
variance/covariance values of the 'fixed.x' covariates.

Compare:

 > psi
   y    z    x
y 0.99
z 0.00 1.00
x 0.00 0.00 0.95

and

 > round(cov(d[,c("y","z","x")]), 2)
      y    z    x
y 1.28 0.60 0.52
z 0.60 2.39 1.15
x 0.52 1.15 0.95

0.95 is simply the sample-based variance of x.

Look also at the parameter table:

 > parTable(my.fit)
   id lhs op rhs user group free ustart exo label plabel start   est    se
1  1   y  ~   x    1     1    1     NA   0         .p1. 0.000 0.550 0.032
2  2   z  ~   x    1     1    2     NA   0         .p2. 0.000 1.206 0.032
3  3   y ~~   z    1     1    0      0   0         .p3. 0.000 0.000 0.000
4  4   y ~~   y    0     1    3     NA   0         .p4. 0.639 0.990 0.044
5  5   z ~~   z    0     1    4     NA   0         .p5. 1.191 1.000 0.045
6  6   x ~~   x    0     1    0     NA   1         .p6. 0.950 0.950 0.000

where you can see (last line) that 'x ~~ x' is an 'exogenous' variance,
not free, but fixed to its starting value: 0.950

Yves.

redundant).

Negative variances for (latent) variances are often a symptom of model
misfit. It could be due to the data (in particular when the sample size
is small), or it could just be that the model is not correct.

Yves.

constraints together. Next, you will see the 'univariate' score tests:
what happens if we release one constraint at a time. These are the
modification indices you are looking for.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Lavaan - CFA - categorical variables - the last threshold is strange
messages.subject_clean: Lavaan - CFA - categorical variables - the last threshold is strange
messages.body_plain:
> Indeed, I have several categorical variables and some variables contains 11 categories.

Thresholds are labeled "t1, t2, ...t[nCategories - 1]", which are character strings.  Thus, they are assigned by default (in R) in alphabetical order (i.e., t10 comes alphabetically between t1 and t2, and you can see that the t10 threshold is indeed between the t1 and t2 thresholds).  I'm sure that is just a situation the developer didn't plan for because I doubt many researchers would hesitate to treat an 11-category ordinal variable as continuous.  Rhemtulla et al. showed that you can treat even 7-category ordinal variables as continuous indicators without noticeably attenuated estimates or biased test statistics using robust MLE:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: simsem and semTools updates
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

simsem and semTools are updated in CRAN. Here are the details of the changes:

[June 06, 2016] Latest Update: simsem, Version 0.5-13

This version is available on CRAN. This is simply a maintenance version.

[June 10, 2016] Latest Update: semTools, Version 0.4-12

This version is available in CRAN. The lavaan package changes the elements in parameter table. Thus, some functions were edited according to the changes. Importantly, runMI did not provide correct results in the combination of lavaan 0.5-20 and semTools 0.4-11 or lower. This version fixes the problem, as well as providing the correct results with the presence of exogenous variables. The asymptotic covariance matrix is also added in the multiply-imputed result so lavWaldTest in lavaan or wald in semTools can be used to implement multivariate Wald test. Furthermore, users can run nested model comparison between two multiply-imputed results using anova. It provides the comparison results using method similar to tests of absolute fit (i.e., LMRR, MR, Mplus, and naive methods). However, the accuracy of the methods has not been investigated yet. The other functions that are fixed based on the change in parameter table are efa, longInvariance, measurementInvariance, measurementInvarainceCat, auxiliary, partialInvariance, partialInvarianceCat, and imposeStart.

Two new functions are introduced in this version. Thanks to Jason Rights and Sonya Sterba, poolMAlloc provides a method to pool results from different parcel allocations. Thanks to Ylenio Longo, htmt is used to assess discriminant validity using heterotrait-monotrait ratio. permuteMeasEq is also updated, such as adding the datafun argument to manipulate data before analyzing a model.

messages.subject: Re: DWLS v. Robust?
messages.body_plain:
On 06/13/2016 11:08 PM, Alan Chan wrote:
> Dear Yves,
>
> According to the previous discussion (cfa with categorical variable),
> may I ask so when I report the 'Robust', what is the exact name of the
> estimator? Is it WLSMV?

That is how it is called by Mplus. But it is a misnomer, for two
reasons. It should be called DWLSSS: we use diagonally weighted least
squares (DWLS) for estimation, and a scaled-shifted test statistic (SS),
which replaced the older mean-variance adjusted (MV) test statistic.

In the literature, the estimator is often referred to as 'three stage
robust diagonally least squares', for example in:

Katsikatsou, M., Moustaki, I., Yang-Wallentin, F., & Jöreskog, K. G.
(2012). Pairwise likelihood estimation for factor analysis models with
ordinal data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 56(12), 4243-4258

The robust standard errors are often called sandwich-type robust
standard errors, and the 'robust' test statistic is the one described in
this document:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/WLSMV_new_chi21.pdf

Yves.

You can post general questions (i.e., not software-specific) on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>, which is a much larger forum of SEM experts.  Once you know what method you need to use, you might find the partialInvariance() function in the semTools package useful.

messages.body_plain:
I would recommend running these models (configural/weak/strong)
manually. You can use labels to constrain sets of parameters to be equal
across groups, see: http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

For example, strong invariance for the Holzinger & Swineford model can
be specified as follows:

HS.model.strong <- '
     visual  =~ c(1,1)*x1 + c(l2, l2)*x2 + c(l3, l3)*x3
     textual =~ c(1,1)*x4 + c(l5, l5)*x5 + c(l6, l6)*x6
     speed   =~ c(1,1)*x7 + c(l8, l8)*x8 + c(l9, l9)*x9

     # ov intercepts
     x1 ~ c(i1, i1)*1
     x2 ~ c(i2, i2)*1
     x3 ~ c(i3, i3)*1
     x4 ~ c(i4, i4)*1
     x5 ~ c(i5, i5)*1
     x6 ~ c(i6, i6)*1
     x7 ~ c(i7, i7)*1
     x8 ~ c(i8, i8)*1
     x9 ~ c(i9, i9)*1

     # lv means
     visual  ~ c(0, NA)*1
     textual ~ c(0, NA)*1
     speed   ~ c(0, NA)*1
'

fit.strong <- cfa(HS.model.strong, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
                   group = "school")

Comparing the models can be done using the anova() function, or (if you
need more options), the lavTestLRT() function.

Next, you can allow for partial invariance by setting some equal labels
to be unequal. For example, for the factor loading of x2, you can write

c(l2, l2bis)*x2

And then, you can compare the models again using anova/lavTestLRT.

This will make it more clear what is causing the NAs.

Yves.

Thank you very much. It is very clear!

On Tuesday, June 14, 2016 at 2:27:30 PM UTC+8, Yves Rosseel wrote:
> On 06/13/2016 11:08 PM, Alan Chan wrote:
> > Dear Yves,
> >
> > According to the previous discussion (cfa with categorical variable),
> > may I ask so when I report the 'Robust', what is the exact name of the
> > estimator? Is it WLSMV?
>
> That is how it is called by Mplus. But it is a misnomer, for two
> reasons. It should be called DWLSSS: we use diagonally weighted least
> squares (DWLS) for estimation, and a scaled-shifted test statistic (SS),
> which replaced the older mean-variance adjusted (MV) test statistic.
>
> In the literature, the estimator is often referred to as 'three stage
> robust diagonally least squares', for example in:
>
> Katsikatsou, M., Moustaki, I., Yang-Wallentin, F., & Jöreskog, K. G.
> (2012). Pairwise likelihood estimation for factor analysis models with
> ordinal data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 56(12), 4243-4258
>
> The robust standard errors are often called sandwich-type robust
> standard errors, and the 'robust' test statistic is the one described in
> this document:
>
> http://www.statmodel.com/download/WLSMV_new_chi21.pdf
>
> Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,
I would like to estimate a model with both the measurement and the structural parts.
The measurement part consists of three CFA models that should be fitted on polychoric correlations by means of a least squares estimation method. Date are indeed from three self-report questionnaires with likert-type or dichotomous items (two questionnaires consists of only likert-type items, while one is composed of both types).

If I declare likert items as ordered and code binary items as dummy (0/1), lavaan automatically switches to the WLSMV estimator.

My questions are:
1 - Does it start from a Pearson correlation matrix or calculate polychoric/tetrachoric correlations?
2 - Are the structural model coefficients estimated by means of the WLSMV estimator or a different method?
3 - Is it possible to use different estimators for the measurement and the structural parts? For example, the WLSMV estimator for the former and the robust ML for the latter?

Thank you very much for any advice!

Best regards,
Mauro

messages.subject: Re: Latent Means - MGCFA - categorical variables - loadings
messages.subject_clean: Latent Means - MGCFA - categorical variables - loadings
messages.body_plain:
> I would like to know if the interpretation of the latent means (the intercepts for the latent variables) is the same that with continuous variables?

Which latent variables?  With continuous indicator variables, you model latent common factors and a latent unique factor (with mean fixed to zero) for each indicator.  When you have ordered categorical indicators, you add a third set of latent variables to the model: a latent item-response (assumed to be normally distributed, with mean fixed to zero) underlying each observed item.  The common factors are assumed to be normally distributed, regardless of the distribution of the observed indicators, so the interpretation of common-factor means does not depend on the distribution of your indicators.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Full coverage model estimation
messages.body_plain:
> 1 - Does it start from a Pearson correlation matrix or calculate polychoric/tetrachoric correlations?

lavaan calculates a polychoric correlation matrix and fits the model to it.

> 2 - Are the structural model coefficients estimated by means of the WLSMV estimator or a different method?

diagonally weighted least-squares

> 3 - Is it possible to use different estimators for the measurement and the structural parts? For example, the WLSMV estimator for the former and the robust ML for the latter?

No, you only fit one model that reproduces a covariance matrix as a function of model parameters (as parameterized using LISREL matrices, in this case).  The distinction between a measurement model (which imposes structure on the covariances among observed variables) and a "structural" model (which imposes structure on the covariances among latent common factors) is conceptually useful in some circumstances (e.g., saturating one to detect misfit in the other). But an SEM is really all a structural model, and all parameters are estimated simultaneously.

I think the polychorics, however, are estimated with MLE, and the asymptotic covariance matrix of those polychoric estimates are used as the weight matrix.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Latent Means - MGCFA - categorical variables - loadings
messages.body_plain:
> The intercepts of my categorical variable are fixed to 0 for the two groups. However, the intercepts for the two latents variables are fixed to 0 for the first group but for the second group the intercepts are not equal to 0. If I am not wrong these values are the latent means. And I don't know how I can interpret these values

The same way you would if your items were continuous.  Since there is no implicit scale to the latent variables (because we haven't observed them), it only makes sense to compare them across groups.  So a latent mean difference between groups would be meaningful to interpret.  Because the Group-1 means are already fixed to zero, Mean_g2 - Mean_g1 == Mean_g2 - 0 == Mean_g2 (i.e., you can interpret the Group-2 latent means as a mean-difference compared to Group 1).  If the latent variances in both Groups are 1, they are also standardized latent mean differences (i.e., Cohen's d).  If not, you can either calculate the pooled SD across groups to calculate Cohen's d yourself, or if you can consider Group 1 a control group (or otherwise meaningful reference group), you could interpret the estimated Group-2 mean as a Glass' delta <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_size#Glass.27_.CE.94> because Group-1's latent SD is already fixed to 1.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I wonder what has caused this problem?

We don't know enough about your model to help you figure it out.  Your figure does not indicate what constraints you used to identify this model.  If the first-order factors were negatively correlated and you set the factor loadings for the second-order construct to 1, then that would explain the negative variance (the variance of a 2-indicator construct is essentially just the covariance of the two items).

> My sample size is 75758 with only 3 measured items.
> If I remove the two 1st order latent variables, the algorithm will converge, but it will give CFI and TLI of 1.000. I believe this is very unreliable?

With only 3 items, you only have enough information to just-identify a single factor, which would be a model with 0 degrees of freedom and arbitrarily perfect fit (i.e., no way to test the fit of the model without imposing further constraints).  I'm not sure what hubris leads you to try modeling 3 factors from only 3 items, but I'm guessing you have not imposed enough constraints to identify your model, which is what the warning said about not computing standard errors.  Even if you did impose enough constraints, the model would be statistically equivalent to a single-factor model or to an unconstrained covariance matrix, so I think you need to use more measures of the constructs you want to model.

messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
messages.body_plain:
"cor.ov" provides the model-implied correlations among observed variables in the model.  "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>" provides the model-implied correlations among the latent constructs in the model.  "cor.all" provides the model-implied correlations among observed and latent variables in the model, so you can get the so-called "Structure Matrix".  All of these are calculated using model parameters, not the observed correlations.  "sampstat" provides the observed covariance matrix and mean vector, to which the model was fit. If you extract that and use the cov2cor() function to convert the covariance matrix to a correlation matrix, you should see matching results (unless you have missing data).

I'm not sure why you are concerned with significance tests of the correlations, but those are a function of sample size as well as effect size.  SEM is a way for you to impose a structure that explains why variables are correlated, so although it is recommended to provide the sufficient statistics (means, correlations, and SDs) so that others can reproduce your model results, it is not necessary to test each correlation against a null hypothesis that it is zero in the population.  But if you do, then adjusting the p values for multiple testing is just a way for you to keep the familywise Type I error rate low.  You could read about other methods in the ?p.adjust help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

lavaan's model syntax is a character string that gets parsed into a parameter table.  It is not a formula object, which allows operations like factor() and I() in the formula.  Compare:

> ?formula
> ?model.syntax

Although you can use operators like exp() and log() to specify nonlinear parameter constraints in lavaan's model syntax, you cannot use such operators to transform variables.  All variables must either exist in the data.frame or be latent variables defined within the model syntax.

Am Freitag, 17. Juni 2016 15:39:10 UTC+2 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:
> "cor.ov" provides the model-implied correlations among observed variables in the model.  "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>" provides the model-implied correlations among the latent constructs in the model.  "cor.all" provides the model-implied correlations among observed and latent variables in the model, so you can get the so-called "Structure Matrix".  All of these are calculated using model parameters, not the observed correlations.  "sampstat" provides the observed covariance matrix and mean vector, to which the model was fit. If you extract that and use the cov2cor() function to convert the covariance matrix to a correlation matrix, you should see matching results (unless you have missing data).
>
> I'm not sure why you are concerned with significance tests of the correlations, but those are a function of sample size as well as effect size.  SEM is a way for you to impose a structure that explains why variables are correlated, so although it is recommended to provide the sufficient statistics (means, correlations, and SDs) so that others can reproduce your model results, it is not necessary to test each correlation against a null hypothesis that it is zero in the population.  But if you do, then adjusting the p values for multiple testing is just a way for you to keep the familywise Type I error rate low.  You could read about other methods in the ?p.adjust help page.

Il giorno giovedì 16 giugno 2016 12:24:50 UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen ha scritto:
> > 1 - Does it start from a Pearson correlation matrix or calculate polychoric/tetrachoric correlations?
>
> lavaan calculates a polychoric correlation matrix and fits the model to it.
>
> > 2 - Are the structural model coefficients estimated by means of the WLSMV estimator or a different method?
>
> diagonally weighted least-squares
>
> > 3 - Is it possible to use different estimators for the measurement and the structural parts? For example, the WLSMV estimator for the former and the robust ML for the latter?
>
> No, you only fit one model that reproduces a covariance matrix as a function of model parameters (as parameterized using LISREL matrices, in this case).  The distinction between a measurement model (which imposes structure on the covariances among observed variables) and a "structural" model (which imposes structure on the covariances among latent common factors) is conceptually useful in some circumstances (e.g., saturating one to detect misfit in the other). But an SEM is really all a structural model, and all parameters are estimated simultaneously.
>
> I think the polychorics, however, are estimated with MLE, and the asymptotic covariance matrix of those polychoric estimates are used as the weight matrix.

messages.subject: Testing Measurement Invariance with WLSMVS
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan listserve,

I am testing a multiple group bifactor CFA model with ordered categorical variables and 7 groups and 7600 total cases. I am confused by the robust chi-square test results when using the WLSMVS estimator and polychoric correlations. I have estimated my configural model (with all parameter estimates free to vary across groups) and my weak invariance model (with all factor loadings fixed to the same values across groups, but all other parameter estimates free to vary across groups).

The non-robust and robust chi-square values lead to different statistical inference when testing for measurement invariance. The non-robust chi-square value in the weak invariance model is significantly greater than (by a scaled chi-square difference test) that of the configural model. Usually this would lead me to reject the weak invariance model and search for partial invariance. However, the robust chi-square value in the weak invariance model is LESS than that of the configural model. Usually this would lead me to accept the weak invariance model and test for strong invariance.

Which set of chi-square values do I compare for statistical inference:  the non-robust or robust ones?

I am not sure if this is something unique to the WLSMVS estimator in lavaan or not. I have never heard of a constrained model having a smaller chi-square value than its associated freed model.

Any advice is appreciated,
David

messages.subject: Re: Basic question: "cor.ov"
messages.body_plain:
> Just to be sure, so "model-implied" means this is how they should correlate if my model was correct?

Yes, if the parameter estimates are the true population values, then the model-implied correlations are the population correlations.

> So if I don't have explicit hypotheses regarding the correlations I shouldn't report whether or not they were significant? I figured since a relationship between the variables is to some extent the basis of my regressional assumptions, it would make sense to do so.

I don't think any reviewer would expect you to do both a correlation and regression analysis on the same variables.  A simple regression slope will have the same p value as bivariate correlation because a correlation is a standardized regression slope.  But once you have multiple predictors of an outcome, then you have potential multicollinearity and suppression that make regression slopes more analogous to semipartial correlations.

messages.subject: Re: Testing Measurement Invariance with WLSMVS
messages.body_plain:
> Which set of chi-square values do I compare for statistical inference:  the non-robust or robust ones?

Typically you use the robust estimator because its Type I error rates are not inflated as non-robust estimators.

> I am not sure if this is something unique to the WLSMVS estimator in lavaan or not. I have never heard of a constrained model having a smaller chi-square value than its associated freed model.

You don't directly compare the scaled chi-squared statistics.  Instead, you calculate the difference between the unadjusted chi-squared statistics of the two models, then scale that (delta-)chi-squared.  The anova() method or lavTestLRT() do this for you automatically.  In some cases, you can get a negative result (which doesn't make sense), so as the ?lavTestLRT help page states, you can set method = "satorra.bentler.2010" to ensure a positive statistic.

messages.subject: Re: use of "update" in lavaan ?
messages.body_plain:
> Can anyone help me with an example of how the "update" function is used in lavaan, and its syntax? ... It is a bit tedious to repeat the full model code everytime i want to test an inclusion/exclusion ... In glm, the "update" function can be used for easy extension/reduction of the model - is the same possible in lavaan?

Unfortunately not.  Because lavaan's model syntax is a character string, not a formula object, you can't use the cool tricks for updating a formula by specifying what to take out or leave in.  But there is a nice shortcut that lavaan's syntax parser allows.  Instead of specifying every parameter in a single character string, you can provide a vector of character strings that lavaanify() concatenates before it parsing it into a parameter table.  So if you have a "Core" model of parameters that will always be specified, you can specify that in one string, then specify a list of all the other additions you might make to that model:

> coreModel <- '
>   ## important shit
> '
> addList <- list(model1 = 'add stuff',
>                 model2 = 'add another
>                           set of stuff',
>                 model3 = 'a third set
>                           of additional parameters
>                           that may or may not
>                           include parameters in the
>                           first two sets')

Then you can loop over the list of additional parameters to update the object with new syntax, saving each result in another list:

> fit <- lavaan(coreModel, data)
> ## fit new models
> newFit <- lapply(addList, function(x) update(fit, model.syntax = c(coreModel, x)))
> ## inspect results for each new model
> sapply(newFit, fitMeasures)
> sapply(newFit, coef)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> ...from your experience, what is todays "gold standard" of testing indirect effects?

I usually see citations for Kris Preacher and Andy Hayes supporting bootstrapping, but I have run small-scale simulations to demonstrate Monte Carlo techniques, and Sobel test seems to perform at least as well as bias-corrected bootstrap CIs even when N = 100 and using 3000 bootstraps.  So the articles Mikko posted definitely do not surprise me, and I think you could cite them to any reviewer who thinks bootstrapping is always preferable (assuming your data are reasonably similar to the conditions described by Koopman et al.).  But this question is better suited for SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>, where you might get a much larger and more diverse set of responses.

messages.subject: Re: Testing Measurement Invariance with WLSMVS
messages.body_plain:
> *The robust chi-square values suggest the weak invariance model fits BETTER than the configural model.

No it doesn't.  The robust/scaled chi-squared test statistic is scaled using an estimated scaling constant that is calculated for that model.  So unless the scaling constants are identical between the two models, you can't compare the scaled chi-squared statistics because they aren't on the same metric.  The robust correction merely transforms the statistic to follow a chi-squared distribution so that the estimated p value will yield approximately nominal Type I error rates.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2013.824793

> I noticed you said you "typically use the robust estimator," so then should I ignore the results of the scaled chi-square difference test and simply compare the two robust chi-square values qualitatively?

No, you just need to pay attention to the chi-squared difference test. That is the only valid comparison, because it corrects the 1 statistic that is of interest (the change in chi-squared).  And it is the only result that makes sense because your fit gets worse by definition when you fit a more constrained model.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

See my original response :-)  You can create any user-defined parameters in the bootstrapLavaan() output by using the same definitions you used in the model syntax. > out <- as.data.frame(bootstrapLavaan(..., FUN = coef))
> out$ab <- out$a * out*b
> quantile(out$ab, probs = c(.025, .975))

Note that if you want a bias-corrected, accelerated CI, you can define a function that accepts your data frame and an arbitrary index variable to extract rows in a bootstrap sample, then fits the model and returns the coefficients, including (or only returning) the indirect effect.  Then you could use the boot() function directly (from the boot package), enabling you to extract the BCa CI using the boot.ci <http://boot.ci>() function.

messages.subject: Modeling an Endogenous Covariate in simsem
messages.subject_clean: Modeling an Endogenous Covariate in simsem
messages.body_plain:
The syntax below give the error massage:"Error in names(coef) <- lab :   'names' attribute [23] must be the same length as the vector [20]."How to solve the problem, or is there a bug?

library(simsem)

# First analysis model: Model without covariate

popModel <- "
f1 =~ 0.6*y1 + 0.6*y2 + 0.6*y3
f2 =~ 0.6*y4 + 0.6*y5 + 0.6*y6
f3 =~ 0.4*y1 + 0.4*y2 + 0.4*y3 + 0.4*y4 + 0.4*y5 + 0.4*y6 + 1*y7
f2 ~ 0.4*f1
f1 ~~ 0*f3
f2 ~~ 0*f3
f1 ~~ 1*f1
f2 ~~ 1*f2
f3 ~~ 1*f3
y1 ~~ 0.64*y1
y2 ~~ 0.64*y2
y3 ~~ 0.64*y3
y4 ~~ 0.64*y4
y5 ~~ 0.64*y5
y6 ~~ 0.64*y6
y7 ~~ 0*y7
"
# Second analysis model: Model accounting for covariate in the indicator level

analyzeModel2 <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6
f3 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6 + 1*y7
f2 ~ f1
f1 ~~ 0*f3
f2 ~~ 0*f3
f1 ~~ 1*f1
f2 ~~ 1*f2
f3 ~~ f3
y1 ~~ y1
y2 ~~ y2
y3 ~~ y3
y4 ~~ y4
y5 ~~ y5
y6 ~~ y6
y7 ~~ 0*y7
"

Output2 <- sim(1000, n=200, analyzeModel2, generate=popModel, lavaanfun="lavaan")
summary(Output2)

The syntax is from https://github.com/simsem/simsem/blob/master/SupportingDocs/Examples/Version05/ex16/ex16.R

messages.body_plain:
> It is possible to compare two different models (one-factor model Vs. three-factor model) across two groups (e.g. males Vs. females)?

You only get one set of fit measures for the model, even if it is a multiple-group model.  Perhaps all you mean is that you want a different model fit to the two groups (perhaps so you can compare it to a model with the same factor structure)?  In your case, a one-factor model is equivalent to a 3-factor model in which all factor variances are equal (ideally, just fix them all to 1) and all factor correlations are fixed to 1.  You will get a warning message that the latent covariance matrix is not positive definite (NPD), but you can ignore it because you are making it NPD on purpose.

messages.subject: Re: How are the path coefficient estimates calculated?
messages.subject_clean: How are the path coefficient estimates calculated?
messages.body_plain:
If the model fit the data perfectly, then the path between the two factors would be exactly equal to the covariance of the factors, or the covariance between the communalities of the two sets of observed variables. If the model is estimated from sample data using maximum likelihood (ML), then the path is a ML estimate of the covariance between communalities, accounting for random sampling error. If the model does not fit exactly, then the path is equal to the value that best minimizes ML lack of fit, given the model's constraints. That is the estimation machinery you are using.

messages.subject_clean: default sample size used when bootstrapping?
messages.body_plain:
> What sample size does lavaan draw per default from my inital sample when I bootstrap with se = "boot"?

By definition, it is only bootstrapping if the same sample size is drawn (with replacement).  Drawing only a subset of the sample (albeit without replacement) would be a leave-k-out technique, like the jackknife (leave-1-out).

> Can I define the sample size for each bootstrap iteration?

No.  Although it is possible to imagine a method in which subsets are resampled with replacement, I am not aware of any such method having been developed:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1207/S15327906MBR3404_2

messages.subject: Re: default sample size used when bootstrapping?

messages.body_plain:
Terrence,

hm?? https://www.amazon.com/Subsampling-Springer-Statistics-Dimitris-Politis/dp/0387988548
-- that stuff has been around for a couple of decades.

Subsampling (drawing samples with replacement of the size smaller than
the original sample) is a common technique that is used when the
"mainstream" bootstrap fails. This happens in many irregular problems
(see e.g. http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cjs.5550340103/abstract),
so basically the situation where the bootstrap definitely works
properly is limited to the confidence intervals for the mean of the
i.i.d. data (well... if the underlying distribution *does* have a mean
-- Cauchy doesn't, for instance). Nearly any other situation requires
an actual proof that the bootstrap works. Subsampling works by adding
another layer of asymptotics and potentially a special rate of
subsampling (say subsample size k=O(n^{1/3}) or something like that)
when the rate of convergence for the statistic in question makes the
"mainstream" bootstrap fail.

Awkward bootstrap situations in the SEM include testing the overall
fit (for which the Bollen-Stine modification, which should have been
called Beran-Srivastava modification, exists) and testing the zero
variances (and that just fails miserably, at any rate
http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150; with references to
Donald Andrews' work on the bootstrap for the boundary situations).
What I continue to be personally uncomfortable with in SEM methodology
are situations where the covariance degrees of freedom exceed the
sample sizes (say a model with 30 variables and {30 \choose 2} = 435
covariances and sample size n=300). I suspect (but can't really
pinpoint) small sample problems in these situations. Any of the
mainstream bootstrap (that on average takes 63.2% of the original
sample points; http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/96739/5739) or
subsampling (that intentionally reduce the sample size) would
potentially only make matters worse. There's a trove of dissertation
research in figuring that stuff out, but it would end up too technical
for the SEM journal but not of general interest to JASA.
